title: Beginner Pack 3
subtitle: Living Beings, Joining Nouns & Past Facts
label: 3 patterns · 6 questions
rationale: Builds directly on Pack 1’s existence, noun-linking, and copula patterns: (1) A に B が います completes the animate/inanimate contrast introduced with Pack 1’s あります using Level 1 people counters (一人, 二人, 三人), (2) A と B joins two equal nouns (“A and B”) in contrast to Pack 1’s modifier A の B, and (3) A は B でした shifts Pack 1’s A は B です into the polite past.
description: Describe where people are with います, join nouns with と (“and”), and talk about the past with でした (“was / were”).

patterns.pattern: A に B が います
patterns.gloss: There is B in/at A (people & animals)
patterns.readingNote: Use います for living people and animals; use あります (from Pack 1) for non-living things.
patterns.summary: Use Location に + Person/Animal が います to say that a living being (B) is at a place (A). People counters like 一人 (ひとり), 二人 (ふたり), or 三人 (さんにん) can go right before います.

examples.japanese: 入り口に人が二人います。
examples.reading: いりぐちに ひとが ふたり います。
examples.gloss: 入り口 entrance · 人 person · 二人 two people · います there are (living)
examples.english: There are two people at the entrance.

examples.japanese: へやに大人が三人います。
examples.reading: へやに おとなが さんにん います。
examples.gloss: へや room · 大人 adult · 三人 three people · います there are (living)
examples.english: There are three adults in the room.

questions.prompt: Choose the verb that completes “There are two people at the entrance”:
questions.targetMeaning: There are two people at the entrance.
questions.reading: いりぐちに ひとが ふたり（　）。
questions.gloss: 入り口 entrance · 人 person · 二人 two people

choices.explanation: That’s right! People (人) are living beings, so we use います (“There are two people at the entrance”).
Not quite. あります is only for non-living things (like desks, boxes, or entrances), whereas people (人) take います.
Not quite. 下げます (さげます) means “to lower something,” not “there are.”

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — Choose the verb that completes “There are three adults in the room”:
followUp.targetMeaning: There are three adults in the room.
followUp.reading: へやに おとなが さんにん（　）。
followUp.gloss: へや room · 大人 adult · 三人 three people

choices.explanation: Not quite. あります is used for non-living things; living people like 大人 (adults) require います.
That’s right! Adults (大人) are living people, so います completes “There are three adults in the room.”
Not quite. 上げます (あげます) means “to lift / raise something,” not “there are.”

workedExample.japanese: へやに大人が三人います。
workedExample.reading: へやに おとなが さんにん います。
workedExample.english: There are three adults in the room.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: へやに marks the place (“in the room”). Step 2: 大人が三人 names the living people and count (“three adults”). Step 3: Use います (never あります) for living beings.

questions.japanese: 駅の入り口に女の人が一人います。
questions.reading: えきの いりぐちに おんなの ひとが ひとり います。
questions.gloss: 駅 station · 入り口 entrance · 女の人 woman · 一人 one person

choices.text: There is one entrance at the station.
choices.explanation: Not quite. 駅の入り口に marks the location (“at the station’s entrance”), and 女の人が一人います means “there is one woman.”

choices.text: There are two women at the station’s entrance.
choices.explanation: Not quite. 一人 (ひとり) means “one person,” whereas “two people” is 二人 (ふたり).

choices.text: There is one woman at the station’s entrance.
choices.explanation: That’s right! 駅の入り口に sets the location (“at the station’s entrance”), 女の人が一人 names “one woman,” and います states she is there.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — What does this new sentence mean?
followUp.japanese: ビルの下に人が三人います。
followUp.reading: ビルの したに ひとが さんにん います。
followUp.gloss: ビル building · 下 under / below · 人 person · 三人 three people

choices.text: There are three people below the building.
choices.explanation: That’s right! ビルの下に marks the location (“below the building”), 人が三人 means “three people,” and います states they are there.

choices.text: There are three buildings below the person.
choices.explanation: Not quite. In ビルの下に, 下 (“below”) is the head noun modified by ビル (“below the building”), and 人が三人います means “there are three people.”

choices.text: There are two people above the building.
choices.explanation: Not quite. 下 (した) means “below” (not 上, “above”), and 三人 (さんにん) means “three people” (not 二人, “two people”).

workedExample.japanese: ビルの下に人が三人います。
workedExample.reading: ビルの したに ひとが さんにん います。
workedExample.english: There are three people below the building.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: ビルの下に = “below the building” (location + に). Step 2: 人が三人 = “three people” (living noun + が + people counter 三人). Step 3: います = “there are” (for living beings).

patterns.gloss: A and B (complete list of nouns)
patterns.readingNote: と joins nouns only (“mountain and river”); it cannot join two whole sentences.
patterns.summary: Place と between two nouns (A と B) to list them together as “A and B,” in contrast to の (which makes A modify B).

examples.japanese: あそこに山と川があります。
examples.reading: あそこに やまと かわが あります。
examples.gloss: あそこ over there · 山 mountain · と and · 川 river · あります there are
examples.english: There are a mountain and a river over there.

examples.japanese: テーブルの上にりんごと箱があります。
examples.reading: テーブルの うえに りんごと はこが あります。
examples.gloss: テーブルの上 on the table · りんご apple · と and · 箱 box
examples.english: There are an apple and a box on the table.

questions.prompt: Choose the particle that joins 山 (mountain) and 川 (river) to mean “a mountain and a river”:
questions.japanese: あそこに山（　）川があります。
questions.targetMeaning: There are a mountain and a river over there.
questions.reading: あそこに やま（　）かわが あります。
questions.gloss: あそこ over there · 山 mountain · 川 river

choices.explanation: Not quite. 山の川 uses の to make 山 modify 川 (“a mountain river”), rather than listing “a mountain and a river.”
That’s right! と joins the two nouns 山 and 川 as equal items: “a mountain and a river.”
Not quite. を marks the direct object of an action verb and cannot join two nouns before あります.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — Choose the particle that joins りんご (apple) and 箱 (box) to mean “an apple and a box”:
followUp.japanese: テーブルの上にりんご（　）箱があります。
followUp.targetMeaning: There are an apple and a box on the table.
followUp.reading: テーブルの うえに りんご（　）はこが あります。
followUp.gloss: テーブルの上 on the table · りんご apple · 箱 box

choices.explanation: Not quite. を marks the object of a transitive verb, not a pair of nouns.
Not quite. りんごの箱 means “an apple box / box of apples” (one thing modifying the other), not “an apple and a box.”
That’s right! と links りんご and 箱 together as “an apple and a box.”

workedExample.japanese: テーブルの上にりんごと箱があります。
workedExample.reading: テーブルの うえに りんごと はこが あります。
workedExample.english: There are an apple and a box on the table.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: Place と between the two nouns りんご (“apple”) and 箱 (“box”) → りんごと箱 (“an apple and a box”). Step 2: Follow with があります (“there are”).

questions.japanese: へやに机と箱があります。
questions.reading: へやに つくえと はこが あります。
questions.gloss: へや room · 机 desk · と and · 箱 box

choices.text: There are a desk and a box in the room.
choices.explanation: That’s right! へやに means “in the room,” 机と箱 joins “a desk and a box” with と, and あります states they are there.

choices.text: There is a box on the desk in the room.
choices.explanation: Not quite. “On the desk” would be 机の上に, whereas 机と箱 joins the two nouns with と (“a desk and a box”).

choices.text: Please give me a desk and a box.
choices.explanation: Not quite. “Please give me” uses を下さい, whereas があります means “there is / there are.”

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — What does this new sentence mean?
followUp.japanese: りんご一つとみずを下さい。
followUp.reading: りんご ひとつと みずを ください。
followUp.gloss: りんご一つ one apple · と and · みず water · 下さい please give me

choices.text: There are one apple and water here.
choices.explanation: Not quite. 下さい means “please give me,” not “there are” (あります).

choices.text: Please give me one apple and water.
choices.explanation: That’s right! と joins りんご一つ (“one apple”) and みず (“water”), and を下さい politely asks “please give me.”
Not quite. 一つ (ひとつ) is “one,” and とみず adds “and water.”

workedExample.japanese: りんご一つとみずを下さい。
workedExample.reading: りんご ひとつと みずを ください。
workedExample.english: Please give me one apple and water.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: Join the two requested nouns with と: りんご一つとみず (“one apple and water”). Step 2: Add を下さい (“please give me”).

patterns.pattern: A は B でした
patterns.readingNote: です is present/non-past (“is”); でした is the polite past (“was / were”).
patterns.summary: Replace です with でした at the end of a noun sentence to say what something was in the past (“A was B”).

examples.japanese: ここは駅の入り口でした。
examples.reading: ここは えきの いりぐち でした。
examples.gloss: ここ here · 駅 station · 入り口 entrance · でした was
examples.english: Here was the entrance to the station.

examples.japanese: きのうはいい日でした。
examples.reading: きのうは いい ひ でした。
examples.gloss: きのう yesterday · いい日 good day · でした was

questions.japanese: ここは駅の入り口でした。
questions.reading: ここは えきの いりぐち でした。
questions.gloss: ここ here · 駅 station · 入り口 entrance · でした was

choices.text: Here is the entrance to the station now.
choices.explanation: Not quite. Present “is” uses です (入り口です), whereas でした is the polite past (“was”).

choices.text: Here was the entrance to the station.
choices.explanation: That’s right! ここは駅の入り口 names “the entrance to the station,” and でした places it in the past (“was”).
Not quite. 入り口 is the noun “entrance” and でした means “was,” not a request.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — What does this new sentence mean?
followUp.japanese: あそこはホテルでした。
followUp.reading: あそこは ホテル でした。
followUp.gloss: あそこ over there · ホテル hotel · でした was

choices.text: Over there is a hotel now.
choices.explanation: Not quite. Present “is” would be ホテルです, whereas でした is the past tense (“was”).
Not quite. There is no question particle か; でした states “was” in the past.

choices.text: That place over there was a hotel.
choices.explanation: That’s right! あそこは sets “that place over there” as the topic, and ホテルでした states that it was a hotel.

workedExample.japanese: あそこはホテルでした。
workedExample.reading: あそこは ホテル でした。
workedExample.english: That place over there was a hotel.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: あそこは marks the topic (“that place over there”). Step 2: ホテルでした uses the polite past でした instead of です to mean “was a hotel.”

questions.prompt: Choose the ending that completes “Yesterday was a good day” (in the past):
questions.reading: きのうは いい ひ（　）。
questions.gloss: きのう yesterday · いい日 good day

choices.explanation: Not quite. です is non-past (“is / will be”), which clashes with きのう (“yesterday”).
Not quite. います means “there is (a living being)” and cannot follow いい日 to mean “was a good day.”
That’s right! Because きのう (“yesterday”) is in the past, いい日でした (“was a good day”) is required.

followUp.prompt: Follow-up check — Choose the ending that completes “Yesterday, here was the reception desk” (in the past):
followUp.japanese: きのう、ここはうけつけ（　）。
followUp.targetMeaning: Yesterday, here was the reception desk.
followUp.reading: きのう、ここは うけつけ（　）。
followUp.gloss: きのう yesterday · ここ here · うけつけ reception desk

choices.explanation: That’s right! きのう (“yesterday”) calls for the polite past copula でした (“was the reception desk”).
Not quite. です is present/future (“is”), whereas きのう (“yesterday”) requires the past form でした.
Not quite. 下さい means “please give me,” not “was.”

workedExample.japanese: きのう、ここはうけつけでした。
workedExample.reading: きのう、ここは うけつけ でした。
workedExample.english: Yesterday, here was the reception desk.
workedExample.breakdown: Step 1: きのう (“yesterday”) tells us the sentence is about the past. Step 2: End the noun predicate うけつけ (“reception desk”) with でした (“was”).

sources: Komorebi Level 1 curriculum (data/level-1.json): kanji 人, 一, 二, 三, 女, 入, 口, 山, 川, 大 and vocabulary 人, 一人, 二人, 三人, 大人, 女, 入り口, 山, 川, 大きい.
